# Copper July 2012 - Weaker equity markets, ongoing worries in Europe and the USA, and as yet limited signs of the anticipated recovery in China all point to doubts over a second half recovery for copper. What is clear is that macro news is the driver of the copper price rather than the market fundamentals. Expectations are that there may be some more significant actions on QE announced this week after the ECB and FOMC meetings that would likely push metal prices higher and out of the current $7300-$7800/t trading range. - The copper market remains on track for another year of deficit in 2012, rising to ~168kt currently as we have tempered our production numbers which has pushed metal stocks days of consumption lower to 47 days compared to 48 days in our last monthly. Uncertainty in the economic recovery capped prices in Q2. As demand improves and stocks are drawn down in H2, we do expect prices to push higher, particularly in the final quarter to average $8020/t ($3.64/lb) for the full year. - The consumption section focuses on those national markets where wire rod is dominant as the primary driver of refined consumption. We look at Canada and Mexico in the Americas, Poland and Russia in Eastern Europe and Indonesia and China in Asia. With the exception of Mexico, and to a lesser extent Russia, refined consumption is performing fairly well so far this year in the majority of these non-traditional national markets. - As the copper concentrate market waited patiently for clear signs of an upturn in demand, representative spot selling terms achieved by miners amidst sparse trading rose marginally in July to $29/t and 2.9c/lb. With the Chinese appetite for spot concentrates still suppressed by unfavourable TCRCs and the continuing negative arbitrage between the SHFE and LME copper prices, the main motivation for buyers has been to secure clean material for blending purposes. Under these circumstances terms have not changed significantly with Chinese smelters buying spot material at terms of $45/t and 4.5c/lb, i.e. close to last month’s levels of $48/t and 4.8c/lb. At present there is no conclusive data either way to suggest how strong any potential economic recovery might be across the major economies. This does leave those of us who look at the financial and metals markets, with more questions than answers at the moment. **Macro news drives copper sentiment** What is clear is that any news, good or bad, is the driver of the copper price rather than the market fundamentals. With no change anticipated over the short term, prices will rise and fall closely in line with the macro economic headlines over the coming weeks much like it has been over the past month. A recent example was the reaction from the market following an announcement from European Central Bank President Mario Draghi on Thursday 26th July that the ECB will do whatever is necessary to protect the euro, which led to an uptick in prices and off the low for the month of $7344/t just the previous day. A short time later reports that jobless Americans filing new claims for benefits fell close to a four-year low, pushed 3-month copper back up above $7570/t. Draghi’s comments have fuelled speculation that some major central banks will move to boost the slowing world economy, while the news out of the USA was seen as a hopeful sign for the labour market in the world's largest economy. The irony is that even though the latest US GDP figure was better than investors' fears it was still weak enough to potentially push the Fed closer to pumping more money into the economy. A GDP figure of 1.5% on an annualised basis is insufficient to change the unemployment picture which is the Fed's concern and mandate. This news alongside other disappointing data sets across the globe and in combination with Draghi’s and other European leaders comments all lean toward further monetary easing. Expectations are that there may be some more significant actions announced this week after the ECB and FOMC meetings that would likely push metal prices higher. #### **Copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 900 12000

**Confidence hit as Chinese GDP slows** Given copper’s alliance to the health of the world economy, is it not surprising that confidence in this market is seriously lacking; producers are increasingly reluctant to commit to projects and consumers do not want to hold inventories across their production chain. Moreover, the fea

rs of contagion within the Eurozone are also creating waves across the rest of the world.  China’s export-driven economy grew by 7.6% in the second quarter of 2012 compared to the same period a year earlier.  This was its slowest pace in three years, confirming expectations of a downward trajectory that leaves full-year growth on course for its softest showing since 1999.  Yet when looking at the copper market, China remains an enigma.  Net imports in June rose for the first month since February.  Imports continue to flow into the country despite the negative arbitrage between the LME and SHFE and as domestic refined production maintains double digit growth of 10.6% (to 2.8Mt according to official figures) through H1 compared to year ago levels.  While it is clear that all this inbound material is not going directly to consumers, two interest rate cuts in the space of a month, along side moves to allow banks to discount borrowing costs by a further 30% will support those who buy copper for speculative reasons.  Material held in bonded warehouse is reported to be at around 600kt.  Whatever the real figure, the key is that there are no signs that these inventories are growing at present. Indeed, we estimate that around 60% of the net imports in June were for consumers with the remaining held in bonded warehouse.  We estimate that over the past few months a higher proportion of net imports had been going into bonded warehouses.  This shift, should it continue, bodes well for a slow but steady recovery in Chinese refined consumption over the coming months.

There was some spot buying from Chinese consumers when prices dipped to various lows throughout July.  However, interest has been generally subdued and premia for imported copper were reported to be softer at between $50-70/t, slightly down from $60-90/t last month.  Fabricators are still reluctant to buy and hold extra stock at a time when price direction remains unclear despite an improvement in their financing situation with the recent interest rate cuts. 

**Rising copper power cable orders are a tangible improvement** The moves by the government, which includes cutting the amount of cash banks are required to hold as reserves, the reserve requirement ratio (RRR), should help to bolster the economy.  Although Beijing has refrained from pumping out another (inflationary) stimulus package similar to the 4 trillion yuan outlay launched during the global financial crisis, demand for copper products related to the government infrastructure program will benefit, particularly as the focus will be on developing the power grid and railway sector.  We understand that demand for wirerod for power cable has increased by around 5-10% in July compared to levels in June.  The larger power cable plants are likely to receive the bulk of the orders from these national projects and are reported to have increased producti

on to similar levels to those in June last year. Monetary easing should also help lift the housing market over the second half, with cheaper mortgages and easier credit availability for developers. Total floor space under construction and completed rose by 17.2% and 20.7% year-in-year in H1 while newly started housing fell by 7.1% year-in-year over the same period. The latest rate cuts should also support a modest sequential recovery in property sales in H2. Any improvement in the housing market will have a positive effect on general consumer goods and in particular on home appliances which will also benefit from the subsidy program on energy saving household electrical appliances that started in June. This subsidy will last for a year and amount to 26.5 billion yuan ($4.2 billion). All of these moves have been taken as a sign by some economic analysts that the government will do everything possible to underwrite growth ahead of a once-a-decade leadership transition starting this autumn. #### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** 600 450

**Supply still a constraint as demand wavers** Our supply/demand outlook for this year remains in a small deficit. It is clear that supply growth remains constrained. We are currently in the middle of the Q2 reporting season but company results available thus far are showing mixed results and lower refined cathode output overall. In addition we continue to track mine projects and a recurring theme is higher capital costs as is a restraint on project development which is not surprising given the uncertain economic environment. Alongside the softer output figures, refined cathode stocks are edging lower across the exchanges (Comex, LME and Shanghai). Exchange stocks fell sharply in Q2 and have built up by a mere 6kt through July. Given a backdrop of a world seemingly on the brink of a recession, a reported exchange stock total of 449kt is small compared to global consumption estimates of 5.2Mt in Q3. Including our own estimates of unreported inventories, we still expect that stocks days to consumption will fall again in Q3 to 49 days and slip further to 47 days during the final quarter of this year, which should provide support for higher prices over the balance of the year. What is also significant is that despite news of grim demand across the traditional copper consuming regions of Europe and the USA, premia levels have been stable. Although copper consumption was not as good as anticipated within the Eurozone and the USA through Q2, demand is not getting worse, despite the general economic lethargy. As is expected during the seaso

nal summer lull, there is limited interest for spot material. However those market players in need of metal inform us that material is not easy to source and they are certainly having to pay a premium for prompt availability. European premia have been quoted in a wide range as a result, to reflect both volumes and immediacy of delivery. Material required for prompt delivery will attract a premium of $100/t although very small parcels have attracted levels as high as $120/t. Those looking for spot material for delivery in August or September will probably have to pay a lower premium of $60/70/t. In the USA spot premia have been quoted around the 6.0-7.0c/lb level, generally unchanged from Metals Market Service Monthly Update - July 2012 Page 3 of 22 Copper Monthly Update last month. As Kennecott’s refinery steps up its production following its maintenance closures we would expect premia to slip back slightly. #### **Copper spot premia ($/t)** 180 10

**Automotive remains the strongest end-use sector** One positive for copper has been the surprising strength of demand from the automotive sector across North America, Japan, Germany (the sole European contender) and China. Even though this end-use sector only accounts for around 15% of global refined consumption, it has been a key driver of wire and cable and flat rolled production. In China, where automotive production in June rose by 9.1% year-on-year and by 4.1% in the year to June, declining petrol prices and a subsidy program (for small sized engines) have also encouraged sales. That said the larger tonnage end-use markets, construction and electrical appliances, remain uninspiring. Even though the latest US home sales data suggests an uneven recovery, demand for building wire and residential and commercial tube is slow. It is however the non-traditional markets that are flying the banner for the red metal. Demand in Latin America, the ASEAN countries, Turkey and the Gulf are all growing and becoming increasingly important as copper consumers. Indeed these non-traditional countries, including China now account for just over 50% of the refined market compared to around 20% in 2000. Some of them may be suffering from the domino effect of weaker growth across the USA and particularly Europe, however, we do expect to see their share of refined consumption increase as they develop their semi manufacturing sectors and build domestic infrastructure further in the coming years. #### **Refined consumption by industrialised and emerging consumers** 68%

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - July 2012 Page 4 of 22 Copper Monthly Update **Substitution pressures limited by tight aluminium wire rod supply** The challenges posed to the global aluminium industry over the last nine months by the adverse combination of falling LME prices and rising electricity tariff costs have been an unexpected bonus for the copper industry from a substitution perspective. After increasing at double digit rates of 10-15% through H1 2011, EC grade aluminium wire rod supply has slowed abruptly, declining by 0.5% in the last 12 months, although growing by 3.0% in H1 2012. Aluminium smelter closures and idlings, as well as the Rio Tinto Alma strike in Canada and production outages due to industrial accidents, have all conspired to reduce aluminium wire rod supply, especially if the rod line is integrated and fed with hot metal from a smelter. Acute shortages in the North American market have forced consumers to import aluminium wire rod from a variety of distant sources such as Argentina, Iceland, Russia, Oman, Bahrain, India and China to meet their needs despite 24/7 production from other US mills. Not only have logistics become much more complicated, but imports have also come at a price with consumers apparently paying rod premiums of $700-800/t to secure spot supply through H1 2012 according to traded prices. #### **Copper to Aluminium price ratio** 4.15

**Copper:Aluminium price ratio reaches new record** The copper aluminium price ratio hit an all time daily high of 4.15:1 on June 29th as copper prices surged and aluminium continued to weaken. The price ratio and the differential is an important consideration for consumers evaluating switching materials. However, the biggest enabler of actual substitution is the physical availability of aluminium rod. Expanded aluminium rod supply - greater than that required by the considerable volume demands of the booming bare aluminium overhead conductor market - represents the greatest medium and long-term substitution threat to refined consumption growth in insulated wire and cable applications across most geographical markets. Noranda announced in the past week that it will invest to build another wire rod mill in the US. “The new rod mill and the port expansion project are attractive to us because they provide avenues for revenue growth and increased productivity and because their value-creation is largely independent from LME al

uminium prices,” said Layle K. (Kip) Smith, Noranda's President and CEO. "Redraw rod has been one of our strongest primary aluminium products in recent periods, and we expect continued growth in this product.” However, full production will not be achieved until 2015. Some believe that at these current trading levels the copper price is fundamentally too high. It is clear that when prices fell to lows of around $7200/t in June, interest for material perked up. Although lower prices will not encourage producers to bring on projects, they will have a more positive impact on demand, reducing consumers’ working capital and stock financing while also aiding copper on the substitution front. The copper market remains on track for another year of deficit in 2012. This has increased slightly rising to ~168kt currently as we have tempered our production numbers thereby pushing metal stocks days of consumption lower to 47 days compared to 48 days in last month’s publication. Uncertainty in the economic recovery capped prices in Q2 and we now forecast an average of $8020/t ($3.64/lb) for the full year. As demand improves and stocks are drawn down in H2, we do expect prices to push higher, particularly in the final quarter of the year. Revisions to mine output has seen our surplus shrink marginally in 2013 to 462kt compared to 506kt last month. Otherwise, we maintain our view on consumption and prices, although with slightly lower production volumes coming through, metal stocks in 2013 will advance to average 53 compared to 54 in our last monthly report. section focuses on those national markets where wire rod is overwhelmingly dominant as the primary driver of refined consumption.  We look at Canada and Mexico in the Americas, Poland and Russia in Eastern Europe and Indonesia and China in Asia.  With the exception of Mexico, and to a lesser extent Russia, refined consumption is performing fairly well so far this year in the majority of these non-traditional national markets.  Poland and Russia highlight that demand developments in Eastern Europe are far move favourable than the dire headlines surrounding the Western European economy.  Canada is sharing fully in the USA’s slow recovery, although conditions are a little more difficult in Mexico so far this year due to weaker power utility infrastructure orders.  Indonesia is the star performer of H1 2012 with a 15-20% surge in rod production for domestic and export markets, although the full year outturn may be closer to 10% as the market cools in H2.  China continues to blow hot and cold depending on the end use sector.  Automotive production is already responding strongly to new sales incentives, but the home appliance and air-conditioning industries are taking extended summer holiday shutdowns as they seek to clear unsold finished good inventories.  But the most encouraging and tangible sign of the yet elusive H2 recovery is a 5-10% upturn in July copper power cable orders in response to a 16% month-on-month rise in fixed asset investment spending in the power grid. This is the most important consuming sector of the Chinese copper demand equation. 

### **Canada** 

**Consumption holds firm** In the face of a steadily improving domestic economy Canadian refined consumption has risen modestly by 1.5% in H1 2012.  GDP is expected to grow by 2% this year and manufacturing output rose at a healthy rate of 5.6% in the year to May.  Vehicle assembly is one of the best performing industrial sectors with total production up 19% to 1.3M units, led by a 29% surge in light truck output.  This has strongly boosted demand for wiring harnesses and winding wire for auto electric motors, both of which are primarily met by imports from manufacturers in the USA and Mexico. 

**Strengthening construction and utility end use sectors** There are also encouraging signs in the construction sector with building permit approvals for future residential construction rising 9% to 85,500 units in the year to May, compared to 78,200 units in the same period of last year.  In this respect the Canadian market is a step ahead with a noticeable pick up in building wire demand.  By comparison in the US there is the belief that the recession in the construction industry has come to an end, but there are as yet only a few tangible signs that this has been translated into increased physical demand.  Building wire demand is reported to have stabilised through the second quarter but there was equally no upturn in brass mill product shipments to the construction sector.  However, Can

adian demand for utility power cables is growing very strongly in response to a planned 16% year-on-year increase in network capital expenditures to C$21.5 trillion in 2012 after a 2% year-on-year decline in spending to C$18.5 trillion in 2011.  Nexans commented that it had seen double digit organic sales growth in its North American distribution power cable business in H1 2012. 

**Steady growth in copper rod and wire exports** Canadian exports of rod, single strand and stranded wire have expanded steadily, rising 10% to 56kt in the Jan-May 2012 period compared to 51kt in the same period of 2011.  Export volumes have seen unbroken sequential monthly increases since January due to growing shipments to US consumers, which account for 95% of all deliveries.  However, it is unclear whether this trend will be maintained through H2 given the start up of the new SDI-La Farga mill in New Haven, Indiana.  Although 50% of Canadian exports go to wire and cablemakers in New York State, a further 33% of exports go to consumers in the States of Indiana, Ohio, Illinois, West Virginia and Wisconsin.  These are destinations that are reasonable and affordable for deliveries from the new mill by truck so are vulnerable to replacement by expanded US rod production.  SDI-La Farga expects to ship 75% of its production as rod and the remaining 25% as drawn wire.  Canadian imports of rod and wire have also grown and so far in 2012 have risen 14% year-on-year to 31kt while copper tube exports increased this year growing by 12% in the year to May.  Increased local production has also displaced some plumbing tube imports from the United States. 

### **Mexico** 

**Sound economic prospects have yet to stimulate copper demand** Mexican GDP is predicted to expand at a healthy rate of 3.7% this year, slightly lower than the 4.0% increase in 2011.  In Q1 2012, the manufacturing industry grew by 5.5% (7.4%); the construction business by 4.9% (5.8%) and the utilities sector by 3.4% (9.2%) according to the state statistics organisation INEGI.  Unfortunately these were all at lower growth rates than were achieved in the first quarter of 2011 (shown in brackets).  Inflation is manageable at around 4% while interest rates are at historically low and stable levels.  Public debt is quite low - at around 40% of GDP - and with a conservative fiscal policy Mexico has the strong support of the IMF.  However, the downside is that this economic background has largely failed to stimulate the copper intensive sectors of the economy. 

**Lack of tenders for utility products…** The sharp deceleration in growth in the utilities sectors (plus active substitution pressure in telecoms) has probably had the biggest impact on copper demand.  Local cablemaker Condumex attributed the weakness of its Q1 volumes to the reduced number of tenders for power transformers and utility turnkey contracts. Meanwhile on the telecoms side of its business the company noted that although it had benefitted from a 50%

surge in fibre optic cable orders this was at the expense of a 2% contraction in its copper telecom cable volumes and a 23% slump in its coaxial cable shipments.  Energy cable volumes dropped 2% year on year due to disappointing sales of

building wire as a result of the erratic copper price’s effect on distributors order intake.  However, the weakest segment of its business was its brass mill operations where sales dropped by 24% due to weak underlying demand from the construction and HVACR industries.  Substitution losses to plastics and aluminium as well as destocking contributed to the poor outcome.  The outlook for a stronger contribution from the brass mill sector may hinge on a legal challenge from GD (Golden Dragon) Affiliates to the US Department of Commerce to rescind its antidumping duties on US bound seamless copper tube exports from its Mexican plant.  This would enable Golden Dragon to increase its sales to the US market in advance of the opening of its new tube mill in Alabama in late-2013/early-2014. 

**…but the automotive sector outperforms** The motor vehicle assembly sector and the auto components industry that supports it are the main growth segments in 2012.  Total vehicle output rose by 13% year-on-year in H1 2012 to 1.5M units with healthy increases across all of the car, light truck and medium/heavy track sectors.  In addition to this growth in local demand, Mexico also posted an 18% year-on-year rise in wiring harness export volumes in the Jan-Apr period, to serve the expansion in vehicle assembly in the United States.  This continuing market growth has prompted some inward investments to expand local assembly capacity.  Sistemas De Arneses K&S Mexicana, a subsidiary of Sumitomo Electric Industries is currently expanding its existing factory on the border between the states of Aguascalientes and San Luis Potosi while constructing a new factory.  Meanwhile Yazaki is relocating two of its Mexican wiring harness assembly plants to lower cost locations within the state of Chihuahua during 2012 as well as establishing a brand new facility there during 2013. 

### **Russia** 

**Russian consumption is a taxing issue…** Until the end of 2008 Russia had a 10% tax on exports of copper cathode but this was suspended amid the global financial crisis in a bid to support refined production as domestic demand slumped.  Domestic consumption of copper dropped sharply as it became more attractive to ship cathode directly to consumers rather than convert it into wire rod for export.  When the tax was reintroduced at the start of 2011, the trend was reversed, with cathode exports slumping by c.255kt.  At the same time, domestic production of wire rod surged, as did exports of wire rod, and this resulted in Russian consumption of copper jumping by 59% to 708kt, just above levels prior to the suspension of the tax.

**...which leaves demand watchers starry eyed** The net result of these tax changes has been to produce an unusual pattern to Russian refined copper consumption very much like The Plough constellation over the past few years, but we now expect demand to settle into a more typical trend. There has been an announcement of a variable cathode export tax, with no duty levied at prices up to $6000/t, at 10% up to LME prices of $8000/t but at $800/t plus 30% of prices above $8000/t. There is also now a 7.5% duty on exports of wire rod to eliminate any advantage to shipping rod as a proxy for cathode. The introduction of the 7.5% tax on wire rod exports still means that overseas shipments of rod could still be profitable if the cost of producing rod is less than 2.5% of the copper price, which it is at current prices. So far this year, exports of wire rod have performed reasonably well in the face of sluggish demand in key neighbouring markets. Shipments are down only c.5% in the first five months of the year at 140.8kt, although this still compares favourably with 66kt in the January to May period of 2010. However, year to date exports of refined copper are up 43% at 106kt. With exports of cathode rising and rod down moderately, the conclusion is that there has been a decline in domestic apparent consumption so far this year. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - July 2012 Page 8 of 22 Copper Monthly Update **Sluggish semis exports weigh on refined demand** The impact of export tariff changes has masked what was a decent year for Russian demand in 2011. Construction activity and infrastructure spending increased solidly last year, in particular in the second half, after a slump in the wake of the financial crisis. However, in line with economic activity across Europe as a whole, investment is being reined in and this is likely to temper activity in the second half. Despite the firm start to the year for some end use markets in Russia, weakness pervades elsewhere and allied to sluggish export markets, total refined demand has declined. Given that wire and cable producers such as Tele-Fonika and Leoni have plants in Poland, it seems reasonable to suggest that the rod they source is produced domestically, of which Tele-Fonika is by far the largest consumer. However, Tele-Fonika has seemingly tweaked its strategy and product mix over the past few years in favour of aluminium rod and this has resulted in their consumption of copper declining. Leoni assembles wiring harnesses from their Polish plant and exports of these are off slightly, down by c.2% in the year to April, although shipments to key market Germany bucked this trend. This fits with what we have heard about German auto producers outperforming other regional car makers. Interestingly, this means that the automotive end use market is still supporting Polish demand even in the face of an expected sharp decline in domestic vehicle production this year. **Exports take up the slack** Over the past few years Polish consumption of wire rod has declined from just under 200kt in 2008 to around 150kt in 2011, although over the same period refined copper demand has edged slightly higher to Metals Market Service Monthly Update - July 2012 Page 9 of 22 Copper Monthly Update 247kt last year from

237kt in 2008.  The shortfall in domestic end use demand was met by an increase in exports of rod overseas to near neighbouring countries, with Germany, the Czech Republic and Hungary key destinations for Polish rod.  Unlike Russia, exports of wire rod from Poland have actually grown in the first part of the year, and are up by 5% in the January to April period to 46kt.  Polish exports of rod have not been artificially boosted by changes to export tariffs but have benefited from firm growth to key export markets as noted above. 

**Strong start leads to FY upgrade** Although exports of wire rod have performed solidly this year, we understand that domestic demand has fared less well, although still on a par with 2011.  Given the broadly negative backdrop across Europe this is perhaps quite a positive outturn.  Poland has benefited from significant investment in construction over the past few years with European Union funds and building ahead of the Euro 2012 football tournament boosting activity. However, construction is now slowing, although from a reasonable base, while the automotive market also remains steady.  Looking to the future, growth is set to be supported by the power sector owing to the requirement for major investment in generation and the grid, although this is unlikely to come through in significant volumes this year or even in 2013.  A better than previously expected start to the year has led us to upgrade our Polish forecast and we now expect that refined copper demand will rise by 8% to 266kt in 2012, following the solid first half, before slowing to 3% growth next year. 

### **Indonesia** 

**Strong start to year for Indonesia** The Indonesian copper market recovered strongly in 2010 so it was always going to be difficult to maintain the double digit growth rate that it enjoyed that year and as such the slowdown to a 1% expansion in 2011 represented a year of consolidation.  However, 2012 has started in upbeat fashion, with sharp growth in construction and infrastructure spending boosting domestic demand considerably according to our discussions with local consumers. 

**Exports up along the value chain…** In common with Poland and Russia, wire rod mills account for the majority of Indonesian cathode consumption.  Indonesia has a number of wire rod plants, some of which include integrated wire drawing facilities to serve both the domestic and export markets, with both components performing well so far this year. Indeed, exports, which account for around a third of wire rod output, are up by 15% in the first four months at 22kt, while exports of wire and cable are also running at similarly strong rates.  However, even these impressive shipments are dwarfed by the acceleration seen from wiring harnesses, which have enjoyed a bumper increase, with growth to Japan largely accounting for the 33% jump to 11kt in the January to April period.  The increase is fully explained by the recovery in the Japanese car market following the sha

rp contraction seen a year ago. 

**...but domestic demand also weighs in** Domestic demand for rod has been running at a similar pace, although clearly some of this has been then shipped abroad in the form of wire and cable as we mentioned above.  It is the key construction and electrical infrastructure markets that have been the biggest boost to domestic activity, driven by private investment, while government spending on infrastructure projects has also lent support.  However, the Indonesian market is not totally immune from the global contagion from the euro crisis and sluggish economic activity in general and as a result copper consumption growth has begun to slow in H2.  Following this stronger than expected first half we have lifted our full year forecast and now anticipate growth in the region of c.10% this year, representing total refined copper consumption of 241kt. 

### **China** 

**Economy slows but stimulus measures are announced** Chinese GDP grew at 7.6% in the first half of 2012, its slowest pace since the global recession in early 2009.  However monetary and fiscal stimulus measures are now being taken to boost the economy after Premier Wen Jiabao said the government should “place maintaining growth in a more important position and carry out pre-emptive policy adjustments and fine-tuning more forcefully according to the changing situation”.  The Bank of China has cut interest rates twice since June and the renminbi has fallen to its lowest level against the US dollar this year, suggesting the central bank may tolerate some moderate depreciation to support exporters.  Moreover several incentive schemes have been introduced to boost activity in the important automotive, home appliance, power utility and transport infrastructure end use industrial segments to re-ignite sales to clear unsold inventories and boost production and investment.  There are some early signs that this is already starting to have an effect with the Chinese manufacturing PMI index for July rising to 49.5 from 48.2 in June.  The index is the first significant data for the third quarter and signals that the sequential improvement in the economy in the second quarter may be broadening as the impact of the stimulus measures takes effect and boosts business confidence.  However it is also clear that the government no longer has the freedom of manoeuvre to deploy the large scale stimulus that it did in 2009. 

**Automotive sector sparks into life** The clearest sign of an immediate and tangible improvement in end use demand is to be found in the automotive sector.  Total vehicle output rose by 16% year on year in May, and by a further 14% year on year in June, propelling cumulative H1 growth up to 7%.  Moreover, auto wiring harness assembly for export increased at a faster rate of 16%.  The Chinese Association of Automobile Manufacturers said that the industry was stabilising after a significant slowdown in the first four months of the year due to the slack econom

economic climate.  As a result of summer plant closures, Chinese home air conditioner output slumped by 37% to 11.3M units in June from 18.0M units in May.  H1 output has fallen 6% from last year’s sales incentive boosted levels.  It is therefore not surprising that operating rates at Chinese copper tube mills declined in June compared to May.  With little improvement likely before October, downstream consumers have been reluctant to buy cathode priced over RMB56,000/t. 

**Copper power cable orders finally strengthen** In the year to May, total Chinese power cable output rose by a fairly healthy rate of just over 10% to 14.3 M kilometres.  However, because the focus of power utility investment has been in the rural power grid where cables are more often installed aerially, rather than underground in ducts as is more common in urban areas, we understand that aluminium power cable production has been growing at a much faster rate than copper power cables.  This appears to have changed favourably from June with a number of the major power cable manufacturers reporting that they have had been awarded some major copper power cable orders for national projects. This is believed to have been a major factor behind the unexpected 4.35% rise in the wire and cable industry’s capacity utilisation rates in June and tallies with a 16% month-on-month rise in fixed asset investment in the power grid.  As a result, their copper wire rod orders for power cable production have reportedly increased by 5-10% on a monthly basis. Even though their production of power cables has now returned to year-ago levels they are not expecting strong growth for the year as a whole because of the low level of shipments in the first half.  However this does offer the market tangible hope that H2 will be higher than H1 and that Q4 2012 should be considerably better than the weak Q4 2011.

**Scrap imports showing mixed signals for consumers** June copper scrap imports failed to live up to expectations in June, falling 13% from 424kt in May, although this did represent a 12% rise year on year to 369kt gross weight.  This left Chinese H1 scrap imports only 1% higher year on year at 2.2Mt.  With 400kt representing a post-2009 recession monthly average, June gave no indication of any immediate demand for imported scrap from fabricators.  Scrap discounts have narrowed to RMB500-700/t for bare bright copper and consequently buying by fabricators has been conspicuously absent.  Smelters were more active users replacing concentrates with No.2 scrap feed to boost secondary production by over 14% year on year. 

The tightening of the Chinese scrap import policing is most evident in Guangdong province where the customs authorities bolstered by the China Certification & Inspection Group now have a “three 100%” policy, namely copper scrap imports will be 100% weighed, 100% checked and 100% quality inspec

ted. This has even gone as far as emptying containers and unwinding bales to look for undocumented material. The latter has contributed to delays for ships unloading from the US at southern Chinese ports resulting in an extended wait of 45 days for scrap to arrive and clear customs, and then a further 15 days for domestic yards to dismantle and process. But given recent rates of copper price volatility over the full 60 day elapsed period this has greatly heightened commercial risks for Chinese importers. As a result traders have continued to purchase lower copper content No.2 birch/cliff, honey and elmo grades for secondary producers rather than the enhanced price risk of No.1 scrap grades that they source when they are most aggressive and are buying No.1 scrap for fabricators as an alternative to cathode. **Kipoi export deal** Tiger Resources announced that it had entered into an export sales agreement for 30kt/a of copper oxide concentrates at an average grade of 25% Cu from its Kipoi heavy media separation (HMS) plant in the Democratic Republic of Congo to be delivered to China Non Ferrous Metals’ Chambishi smelter in Zambia. The mine, which is located in Luzon in the northern Philippines, is forecast to start production in early 2013 and is forecast to produce 14kt/a of copper in concentrate together with 100koz/a of gold. 

**Codelco environmental investment** Chilean copper producer Codelco announced plans to invest $300M on environmental measures at its El Teniente smelter.  The measures being implemented ahead of proposed new environmental laws in the country are intended to increase sulphur capture from a little over 93% to a minimum of 95% and are believed to comprise construction of a new double contact acid plant and installation of a new primary hood system. ## Production news 

**Production down at Collahuasi** Anglo American reported attributable copper production of 330kt during the first half of 2012, an increase of 14% on the same period in 2011.  However, while total copper production from its Los Bronces mine in central Chile was up by 80% on the previous year at 183kt, reflecting the continued ramp up of the mill expansion from 61 kt/d to 148 kt/d, news was less encouraging from the Collahuasi mine in the north of the country in which Anglo American holds a 44% stake.  Total production at Collahuasi during the first half of 2012 was reported to be 145kt, a fall of 38% on the same period last year.  Although lower head grades were forecast this year, the shortfall was exacerbated by poorer-

than-expected plant recovery, adverse weather conditions, a mine fatality and a further shutdown in order to repair a ball mill.  Collahuasi is seeking to combat falling head grades by increasing plant throughput with an incremental mill expansion from 150kt/d to 160kt/d currently in construction.  Feasibility studies into further and much larger expansions are ongoing and are understood to be due for completion towards the end of this year. 

**Grasberg throughput recovers but head grade remains low** Recoverable copper production at Grasberg reported by Freeport McMoRan for Q2 was 78kt, which was just 66% of the figure achieved over the same period in 2011.  The Q2 performance represented a recovery from Q1 when ongoing labour disputes restricted production to just 56kt of recoverable copper.  During Q2 production rates started to return to normal levels.  Milling rates averaged 180kt/d over the second quarter compared to a target level of 200kt/d and 115kt/d achieved during the first three months of the year. As anticipated, mining activity continued to be focussed on low grade areas of the mine and mill head grades averaged 0.57% Cu compared to 0.77% Cu a year ago.  Forecast total full year production at Grasberg is now estimated to be 380kt compared to 415kt in 2011 with grades scheduled to improve from 2013. 

**Head grade improving at Escondida** BHP reported that total production at Escondida for the first six months of the calendar year amounted to 365kt of copper in concentrate and 167kt of copper cathode.  These figures compare to 294kt of copper in concentrate and 151kt of copper cathode achieved over the same period in 2011 and reflect improved head grades at the mine.  The average grade of ore milled over the first half of 2012 was 1.26% Cu compared to 1.10% Cu in the first half of 2011 and 1.04% copper over 2011 as a whole.  As head grades continue to improve production at Escondida is forecast by BHP to be 20% higher over the next twelve months. 

**Bingham Canyon production set to recover** Rio Tinto reported that first half mine production at its Kennecott Utah Copper Bingham Canyon operation was 61kt, down 42% on the equivalent period in 2011, this was due to planned mining of lower grade areas of the pit.  A 26 day maintenance shutdown at the smelter was completed during the period and mining activity is scheduled to re-enter higher grade areas during the second half at the year.  Reduced output at Bingham Canyon was more than compensated for by the improved grades at Escondida where Rio Tinto’s 30% share of production was 152.3kt, up by 29% on the first half of 2011.  Rio’s 58% share of mine production at Palabora in South Africa was reported to be 18.1kt, down by 13% on the previous year partially in line with lower grades, but also impacted by the failure of a winder at the underground mine in July.  The time required to repair the damage is still under evaluation and is likely to impact production in the second half of the

year.

**Canadian mill re-starts** New Gold announced the start of production at its New Afton copper-gold mine in British Columbia.  The mill is rated to process 11kt/d of ore and will be fed from an underground block cave mine.  The mine and mill are on the site of the Afton open pit, which was mined until 1987 by Teck.  Output from is forecast to peak at 40kt/a of copper in concentrate, with production expected to continue for 12 years based on current reserves. 

**Construction underway at Boschekul** According to local media reports, Kazakhmys has started on-site construction work at its $1.7Bn Boschekul project in northern Kazakhstan.  The project, which is forecast to produce up to 90kt/a of copper in concentrate when it comes on line in 2016, has been partially funded by loans secured from the Chinese Development Bank and it is expected that China will be the destination for the bulk of the plant’s output. 

**Key order placed for Antucoya** Antofagasta Minerals’ Antucoya project, located close to its Michilla mine in northern Chile, took a step towards a scheduled late 2014 start up with news that contracts for the supply of an agglomeration plant, an ‘on-off’ leach pad, and a solvent extraction plant had been signed with Tenova Mining and Metals of Italy. Tenova is an Italian steel company who in recent years has acquired South African eng

ineering company Bateman and the German materials handling equipment supplier Takraf. **Mixed fortunes for developers of Peruvian projects** Anglo American took an important step towards starting construction of its 220kt/a Quellaveco project with news that it had won support from local communities in the Moquegua region in the southern part of the country for its water usage plan. The project still requires construction permits from central government, but the company hopes that work at the site can start later this year. The capital cost of the project is now estimated at $3.3Bn which is understood to include the creation of a $300M social fund that will be used to develop roads, schools, hospitals and hydro-electric facilities in the area. Further north in Peru’s Cajamarca region a 30day state of emergency has been declared in response to violent protests against Newmont’s $4.8Bn Conga copper/gold project where development activity remains suspended. **Iranian expansion plans** Outotec announced the receipt of orders totalling EUR265M for deliveries of equipment to National Iranian Copper Industries Company (NICICO) for expansion projects at its Sarcheshmeh and Miduk mines, a new mine named Nochun and the Khatoon Abad smelter. The expansion at the Sarcheshmeh plant which produced ~170kt of copper in concentrate during 2011 is believed to be rated to add ~45kt/a of additional capacity, while the expansion at the Miduk mine is believed to be of a similar size, effectively doubling output of that facility. Nochun is a greenfield development which, like Sarcheshmeh and Miduk is located in Kerman province in the south east part of the country. The project is understood to be rated to produce ~25kt/a of copper in concentrate plus some by-product molybdenum. The order for the Khatoon Abad smelter is believed to be related to the construction of a sulphuric acid plant at that facility. In 2011 NICICO announced an ambitious $7.5Bn investment program to increase overall copper production from around 200kt/a to 700kt/a.
